title: When Federal Funding Cuts Reach Refugees’ Everyday Lives
displayTitle: When Federal Funding Cuts Reach Refugees’ Everyday Lives
subtitle: How the 2025 suspension of refugee admissions and federal funding changes contributed to CWS Orange County’s closure—and what that means for refugees’ everyday lives in Southern California.
excerpt: After CWS announced its Orange County office would close, I traced how the suspension of refugee admissions and federal funding changes contributed to the decision, and what the closure means for families relying on help with housing, benefit applications and everyday life in Southern California.

content.text: In an email on August 14, 2026, Justin Castillo, senior case manager and volunteer coordinator for the Orange County office of Church World Service (CWS), announced that the agency would close the Orange County office on September 4. Most employees, including Castillo, would end their employment that day, and volunteer-related work would also end.

As fiscal year 2027 (FY27) approached, Castillo described the Orange County office’s situation as a “devastating fiscal cliff.” His closure email cited the suspension of the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program and changes in federal funding, including money being channeled through other organizations. The office also provided services to refugees already in the United States.

content.alt: The U.S. Capitol beneath a blue sky.
content.caption: The U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C. File photograph.

content.text: The policy changes mentioned in the email began more than a year ago. On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14163, titled “Realigning the United States Refugee Admissions Program.” The executive order stipulates that the admission of refugees through the "U.S. Refugee Admissions Program" will be suspended starting from January 27, and the review and approval of refugee applications will be suspended. The executive order allows exceptions to be made on a case-by-case basis and defends the policy on grounds of public safety, national security, community carrying capacity and protection of taxpayer resources.

On the same day, President Trump also signed Executive Order 14169, requiring a review and suspension of foreign development assistance. In response, the U.S. Department of State issued a stop-work notice for resettlement agreements on January 24, including services provided domestically. On February 26, the State Department informed various resettlement organizations that their cooperative agreements would be terminated on February 27. Although the Executive Order on Refugee Admissions restricted refugee admissions, subsequent actions by relevant government agencies further affected the funding of organizations that provided assistance to those already admitted.

In an amended complaint filed in June 2026, Church World Service (CWS) and other plaintiffs noted that part of the per-refugee reimbursement paid to agencies is for direct assistance and the remainder is used to cover service costs and operating expenses. When reimbursement is tied to refugee arrivals, fewer arrivals means less revenue to support agency operations. In addition, freezing payments raises another issue: These organizations may have incurred expenses that they expect the government to reimburse.

In May 2025, CWS announced plans to close 11 local offices, citing changes in federal policy and the loss of related support. The Orange County office was not among those listed. CWS later reported that some services had been restored on May 23 and that most federal funds and reimbursements that had been unavailable had been released.

CWS is one of the plaintiffs in Pacito v. Trump. On March 5, 2026, the Ninth Circuit reversed most preliminary relief for refugee admissions and processing. It kept the orders restoring agreements needed for legally required domestic resettlement assistance. The court said Executive Order 14163 “did not itself terminate the funding of the resettlement programs.” The Department of State had terminated this funding through termination letters.

In a legal filing on August 11, 2026, the government cited restored funding in arguing that the domestic funding claim should be dismissed on the basis that the previous suspension of funding was not expected to reoccur. However, this litigation position does not determine the financial status of each office within the resettlement network.

According to the amended complaint, an Iraqi refugee living in Dallas (pseudonym Ali in the case) arrived in the United States in January 2025 with only $120. The local agency helped him find an apartment. On February 5, the complaint states, he received an email from the Texas Office for Refugees: “there is an indefinite delay in Refugee Cash Assistance benefit payments.” His case manager attributed the delay to a pause in federal funding. He feared losing his home, the complaint states. The complaint also alleges that he later received resettlement benefits after the court issued an injunction.

In addition to the initial refugee reception, the Orange County office was involved in other projects. According to California Department of Social Services records, the CWS Orange County office provided services through the Ukrainian Newcomers Support Program, which uses federal Ukraine supplemental appropriations provided through state grants. These services include case management and housing navigation. The state lists an end date for the program as Sept. 30, 2026.

The program's end date is close to the office's closing date. Neither the state list nor the closing email specified the amount allocated in the office's budget. The announced end date does not prove that the government canceled this funding early. CWS attributes the closure to multiple policy and funding changes; existing records make it impossible to reconstruct the office's budget.

I understood that CWS would finish the help it had already promised as the local arrangements ended. This included housing searches, security deposits and benefit applications. I could not confirm that every payment and case handover was complete.

CWS can help people navigate the CalFresh application, the benefit administered by the Orange County Social Services Agency. The closure of a CWS office does not terminate an individual's eligibility.

CWS's public closure notice states that work begun in Orange County will continue through its Northern California office. It did not specify which clients will receive which services, who will handle their cases, or whether arrangements will be remote or local.
If volunteers and clients want to stay connected, Justin’s closing email leaves them a way to do so as community members rather than CWS volunteers.
